Q9015.L1t: Cells carry out metabolism through networks of chemical reactions that are mostly catalyzed by enzymes.
Q9015.L2t: Enzymes, which catalyze nearly all metabolic reactions, are proteins.
Q9015.L3t: Genes encode the sequences of proteins, so the cell's enzymes, and therefore which reactions it can perform, are set by its genetic material.
Q9015.L4t: Metabolism is determined by the proteins that are made according to the instructions in the genetic material.
Q9015.L2f: Metabolic reactions in cells proceed without enzymes at the same rates, so proteins play little role in them.
Q9015.L3f: The supply of free amino acids in the cell is the limiting factor that sets which metabolic reactions occur and how fast, regardless of which genes are present.
Q9015.L4f: Metabolism is determined by how many amino acids are available to the cell.

Q9016.L1t: The United States has urbanized steadily since the nineteenth century, with most people now living in cities and suburbs.
Q9016.L2t: The Census Bureau defines urban areas by population size and density, and counts both large cities and smaller urbanized clusters.
Q9016.L3t: Census figures show that a little over four-fifths of the U.S. population lived in urban areas in the 2010s, and the share was still below nine-tenths.
Q9016.L4t: In 2017, about four in five Americans, a little over 80 percent, lived in urban areas.
Q9016.L2f: The Census Bureau counts only people living inside the limits of incorporated cities as urban, which leaves out suburban residents.
Q9016.L3f: Census estimates show that nearly all Americans, more than nine in ten, lived in urban areas by the late 2010s.
Q9016.L4f: In 2017, about 92 percent of Americans lived in urban areas.

Q9017.L1t: A joint tenancy with right of survivorship gives co-owners equal undivided interests, and on one owner's death the survivor takes the whole property.
Q9017.L2t: A joint tenancy can be severed by a transfer of one owner's interest, after which the co-owners hold as tenants in common with no survivorship.
Q9017.L3t: In a lien theory state a mortgage only creates a security interest and does not transfer title, so it does not sever the joint tenancy, and the lien ends when the borrowing owner dies and the survivor's interest takes over.
Q9017.L4t: The bank cannot enforce the mortgage, because the lien did not sever the joint tenancy and the surviving partner owns the property outright.
Q9017.L2f: In a lien theory state, a mortgage gives the lender legal title to the property until the debt is paid off.
Q9017.L3f: Under the majority view, any mortgage by one joint tenant transfers title to the lender and so severs the joint tenancy, leaving the lender holding a lien that survives the borrower's death.
Q9017.L4f: The bank can enforce the mortgage, because it severed the joint tenancy and gave the bank title and a lien it can foreclose after the partner's death.
